newsitem.title: USA: U.S. crime mob turncoat tells all in TV interview.
newsitem.headline: U.S. crime mob turncoat tells all in TV interview.

text.p: Salvatore "Sammy the Bull" Gravano, the Mafia turncoat whose testimony put mob boss John Gotti in prison for life, said Gotti once thought he could buy a presidential pardon for up to $5 million.

In a two-part interview with ABC's Diane Sawyer to be shown on Wednesday and Thursday nights and released on Sunday, Gravano said he was sorry for some of the 19 murders he committed -- but not all of them -- and added, "I'm having fun with my life (now). I go in a positive direction."
In his interview with Sawyer, Gravano said that one time before he became a turncoat, he and Gotti were on trial together and discussing how to escape if convicted.

"I said to John, 'If we lose this case ... I'm going out the window. We can escape.' He looks at me and he says, 'Out the window? We're on the 11th floor. What if we fall?' So he says, 'No Sammy, listen to me .... I got another plan. Down the road ... we'll put together four or five million. We'll bribe the president and we'll get a pardon,'" Gravano said.
The interviews to be shown on "PrimeTime Live" and "Turning Point" coincide with the publication of Gravano's biography "Underboss," written by Peter Maas, the author of the bestseller "Serpico."
"I just live a life, like a normal human being should live their life," he said. "I sit down and I smoke a cigar and I relax and I ... love life."
Gravano was underboss in the Gambino crime family headed by Gotti after the two men had Gambino boss Paul Castellano murdered in front of a New York steakhouse on Aug. 29, 1985.

By becoming the highest level mob figure ever to testify against the mob, Gravano received five years in jail and was put into the federal Witness Protection Programme which he has now left, saying he was fed up with its rules. He also said the government let him keep the millions he made illegally and even paid for him to have cosmetic plastic surgery.
He added that because the late Teamsters Union leader Jimmy Hoffa received a pardon Gotti thought there was precedent for him to receive one as well.

Gravano said he decided to testify against Gotti five years ago because he was certain Gotti was about to betray him. He also thought Gotti was destroying the mob by giving it too much publicity and that power had gone to his head.

"Power has a way where you can believe after a while that you can walk on water and I think that's what happened to him," Gravano said. "He was flamboyant. He seemed smart. He seemed nervy. He was a tough guy on the street. And ... he's got charisma. He's got personality. Yeah he impressed me a little bit."

But in the end, he said he thought Gotti was about to let him take the fall for the murders and racketeering charges against Gotti. He said "John's a double-crosser. I'm a master double-crosser. We played chess and he lost."

Gravano admitted to murdering 19 people including his wife's brother and his own best friend. He said, "You can relate me to a soldier in Vietnam who killed hundreds of people maybe. I was a soldier of Cosa Nostra. I am a hitman."

But he added he was sorry for the killings and when asked by Sawyer if he felt pain when he thought about it, he said, "Some of them, sure. Some of them, not all of them, to be honest, not all of them."
Newspaper reports claim there is a $1 million mob contract out for Gravano's death and he said he knew the danger.
"I'm not going to worry about that every single day of my life," he said. "I'm not going to stay in, uh, Montana (or) someplace, scared to death looking out the blinds."
